title: Critical Thinking
description: Size up the claims you meet every day, in news, ads, group chats and meetings: find the real argument, spot the tricks, weigh the evidence and catch your own biases.
keyIdeas: Find the **claim** first, then ask what reasons hold it up, what evidence backs those reasons, and what's quietly assumed.
Many bad arguments dodge the point: they attack a **straw man** or the person, change the subject, or squeeze the options down to two.
Things that move together aren't proof of cause: look for a **third factor**, a reversed arrow or chance.
Small samples swing wildly, and what's **missing** (the failures, the base rate, the starting point) often matters most.
Ask **who says so, how they know and what they gain**, then turn the same questions on your own beliefs.

concepts.label: Main claim
concepts.summary: The conclusion an argument wants you to accept; find it first, before judging anything else.

concepts.label: Reasons and evidence
concepts.summary: Reasons say why the claim should be believed; evidence (facts, data, examples) backs up the reasons.

concepts.label: Hidden assumption
concepts.summary: An unstated link that must also be true for the reasons to support the claim.

concepts.label: If-then reasoning
concepts.summary: From "if P then Q" you may conclude Q from P, or not P from not Q, but not P from Q or not Q from not P.

concepts.label: Straw man
concepts.summary: Twisting a claim into a weaker or more extreme version and knocking that down instead.

concepts.label: Ad hominem
concepts.summary: Attacking the person instead of answering their argument.

concepts.label: Whataboutism
concepts.summary: Deflecting a criticism by pointing to someone else's failing, which changes the subject without answering it.

concepts.label: False dilemma
concepts.summary: Presenting only two options when more exist.

concepts.label: Slippery slope
concepts.summary: Claiming one step will inevitably set off a chain of disasters, with no evidence for the links.

concepts.label: Appeal to authority
concepts.summary: Treating someone's say-so as proof; fine for a relevant expert consensus, a fallacy when they are outside their field or stand to gain.

concepts.label: Correlation vs causation
concepts.summary: Two things moving together doesn't prove one causes the other: look for a third factor, a reversed arrow or chance.

concepts.label: Confounder
concepts.summary: A hidden third factor that drives both things, making them move together.

concepts.label: Reverse causation
concepts.summary: The arrow runs the other way: B causes A rather than A causing B.

concepts.label: Randomised experiment
concepts.summary: Randomly splitting into groups and changing only one thing spreads confounders evenly, so a clear difference is likely caused by the change.

concepts.label: Post hoc fallacy
concepts.summary: Assuming that because B came after A, A caused B.
aliases: after this therefore because of this

concepts.label: Small sample
concepts.summary: Few cases swing wildly by chance, so drawing a big conclusion from them is a hasty generalisation.

concepts.label: Cherry-picking
concepts.summary: Showing only the cases that fit the story and leaving out the rest.

concepts.label: Survivorship bias
concepts.summary: Looking only at what made it through a filter, so the failures that would change the picture are invisible.

concepts.label: Source checking
concepts.summary: Ask who says so, how they know (firsthand or passed on) and what they gain; incentives tell you how hard to check, often by reading other sources.

concepts.label: Confirmation bias
concepts.summary: Noticing and seeking out evidence that fits what you already believe, and shrugging off what doesn't.

concepts.label: Anchoring
concepts.summary: A first number pulls later estimates toward it, even when it is irrelevant.

concepts.label: Steelman
concepts.summary: Restating the other side's view in its strongest form before responding: the opposite of a straw man.

concepts.label: Relative vs absolute risk
concepts.summary: A 50% rise can mean 2 in 1,000 becoming 3 in 1,000; always ask '50% of what?' and count the extra cases.

concepts.label: Base rate
concepts.summary: How common something is to begin with; when it is rare, false alarms from the large majority can swamp the true hits.

units.title: Find the real argument
units.description: Pull a claim apart into its pieces, and check what actually follows.

lessons.title: What are they actually claiming?
lessons.takeaway: Every argument is a claim held up by reasons and evidence; find the claim first, then check what's really holding it up.

steps.title: Meet the group chat
steps.body:
Meet **Flat 4B**: four housemates and one very busy group chat. **Dana** forwards everything, **Leo** loves a debate, **Priya** always asks for a source, and **Sam** believes the best of everyone.

Any message that tries to change your mind is an **argument**, and every argument has the same parts:

- **Claim**: what they want you to believe or do.
- **Reasons**: *why* you should.
- **Evidence**: the facts, numbers or examples that back up the reasons.

Find those three and you can size up almost anything.

steps.prompt:
Leo posts: *"We should switch to the Saver energy plan. It would cut our bills, and their customer service is better. My cousin switched last spring and her bill dropped by $20 a month. Their ad says customers save up to 30%. And a consumer survey rated Saver top for service."*

Sort each piece of his argument.

items.text: We should switch to the Saver plan
It would cut our bills
Their customer service is better
His cousin's bill dropped by $20 a month after switching
Saver's ad says customers save up to 30%
A consumer survey rated Saver top for service

steps.hint: For each piece ask: is it what he wants (claim), why he wants it (reason), or how he knows (evidence)?
steps.explanation:
The **claim** is what Leo wants the flat to do: switch. The **reasons** answer *"why?"*: cheaper bills, better service. The **evidence** answers *"how do you know?"*: the cousin, the ad, the survey.

Notice the evidence isn't equally good. One cousin is a single story, and an ad is the seller talking about itself. The independent survey is the strongest piece. Sorting the parts is what lets you see that.

steps.title: The piece nobody says
steps.body:
Between the reasons and the claim there's usually an unstated link: a **hidden assumption**. It's what must *also* be true for the reasons to support the claim.

Dana: *"This face cream has 4.8 stars from 10,000 reviews, so it'll work for me."*

Hidden assumptions: the reviews are genuine, **and** what worked for those reviewers will work for *her* skin. If either is false, the argument falls apart, even though Dana never said them out loud.

steps.prompt:
Sam: *"The new manager worked at three big companies, so she'll sort out our team's missed deadlines."*

Which hidden assumption does Sam's argument rely on?
choices: What she did at big companies carries over to fixing deadlines on this team
The new manager worked at three big companies
Big companies pay better than small ones
The team asked for a new manager
steps.hint: A hidden assumption is unstated, and the argument collapses without it.
steps.explanation: The reason (three big companies) only supports the claim if that experience **transfers** to this problem. That's the gap worth probing: *what did she actually do there?* The second option is the stated reason, not a hidden one, and the other two aren't needed for the argument at all.

steps.title: Take apart a message
steps.problem: Dana: *"Don't drink the tap water here! My friend's neighbour got sick last week, and the water company was in the news last year for a leak."*
steps: **Claim:** don't drink the tap water here.
**Reasons:** (1) someone got sick; (2) the water company had a problem.
**Evidence:** a third-hand story about one person, and a year-old news item. Neither shows the water is unsafe *now*.
**Hidden assumptions:** the neighbour got sick *from the water* (not food or a virus), and last year's leak still affects today's water.
**Verdict:** weak. A better check: the water company's latest test results, or a notice from the local council.
steps.answer: Claim → reasons → evidence → hidden assumptions → verdict.

steps.prompt: Priya pitches an idea at the café where she works. Put her points in order, from the **starting evidence** up to her **final claim**.
items: Our cinnamon buns sold out before 10 a.m. on 9 of the last 10 days.
So customers want more buns than we're baking.
So a second tray each morning would probably sell too.
So we should start baking a second tray every morning.
steps.hint: Find the claim first: it's the one that tells someone what to do. Then work backwards.
steps.explanation:
Each point leans on the one before it: the sell-outs (evidence) suggest unmet demand (reason), which suggests extra buns would sell (reason), which supports the decision (claim).

There are hidden assumptions too: that sell-outs mean demand rather than just a small batch that people buy because it's there, and that a second tray earns more than it costs. A good manager would ask about both.

steps.prompt:
Leo, again: *"The gym near work is always packed, the showers are cold, and I've only managed three visits this month. I'm cancelling, and you should too. It's not worth $40."*

What's the main claim aimed at **you**?
choices: You should cancel your membership too
The gym is always packed
The showers are cold
He only went three times this month
steps.explanation: The claim is what he wants *you* to do: cancel. Packed and cold are **reasons**; three visits is **evidence** about *his* use. That reveals a hidden assumption: what's true of his habits is true of yours. If you go every day, his argument barely touches you.

lessons.title: Does that really follow?
lessons.takeaway: "If A then B" plus B tells you nothing certain about A; only A, or not-B, lets you conclude something.

steps.title: Safe moves and traps
steps.body:
Lots of arguments run on **if-then**: *If it rained overnight, the pavement is wet.* Suppose that rule is true.

Two moves are safe:
- It rained → so the pavement is wet.
- The pavement is dry → so it didn't rain.

Two moves *feel* safe but aren't:
- The pavement is wet → so it rained. (Sprinklers? A street cleaner?)
- It didn't rain → so the pavement is dry.

The first trap is **affirming the consequent**; the second is **denying the antecedent**.

steps.prompt: Let **P** = *it rained overnight* and **Q** = *the pavement is wet*. Fill in when each rule holds. An if-then rule is broken only when its *if* part happens and its *then* part doesn't.
steps.hint: "If P then Q" is broken only in the row where P is true and Q is false. Every other row keeps the promise.
steps.explanation:
"If P then Q" fails only when it rained but the pavement is dry. The reversed rule fails in a *different* row: wet pavement but no rain, which is exactly the sprinkler case.

Because the columns differ, knowing one rule doesn't give you the other. That's why *"it's wet, so it rained"* doesn't follow.

steps.prompt:
Take this rule as true: **If a message asks you to pay with gift cards, it's a scam.**

For each line of reasoning, does the conclusion **have** to follow from the rule?

items.text: This message asks for gift cards. So it's a scam.
Jo paid a "delivery fee" with gift cards, as the text asked. So that text was a scam.
This message is genuine. So it doesn't ask for gift cards.
This message is a scam. So it asks for gift cards.
This parcel text asks for a bank transfer, not gift cards. So it's genuine.
This message doesn't mention gift cards. So it's safe.

steps.hint: Two moves are safe: the *if* part happens, or the *then* part fails. Reversing the rule, or negating its *if* part, is a trap.
steps.explanation:
**Must follow:** the rule's *if* part happens (gift cards, so scam), or its *then* part fails (not a scam, so no gift cards).

**Doesn't follow:** scams ask for bank transfers, crypto and card details too. The rule only says gift cards → scam, not scam → gift cards. That's the costly one in real life: *"no gift cards, so it's safe"* is exactly how a bank-transfer scam gets through.

steps.title: Think like a detective
steps.body:
Detective work is the same skill: conclude **only** what the clues force.

The most useful safe move in puzzles: *If P then Q* plus *not Q* gives you *not P*. "If Leo took the bus, he had his travel card." "Leo didn't have his card." So Leo didn't take the bus.

Now a real puzzle. Four housemates, four rumours, four sources, and only what the clues force.

steps.prompt: Rumour week in Flat 4B. Each housemate passed on a different rumour, and each heard it from a different source. Work out who said what, and where they got it.

categories.name: Housemate
items: Dana
Leo
Priya
Sam

categories.name: Rumour
items: Café closing
Rent rising
Gym opening
Street party

categories.name: Source
items: Screenshot
Landlord
Local paper
Friend of a friend

clues: Priya didn't pass on the street party.
If Priya's source wasn't the landlord, then she's the one who passed on the street party.
The gym news came from the local paper.
Dana didn't get hers from the local paper.
Leo didn't pass on the café news or the gym news.
If a rumour came from a screenshot, it was about the café.
steps.hint: Start with clues 1 and 2 together: an if-then plus a "not" is the safe move from the last step.
steps.explanation:
Clues 1 and 2: Priya didn't pass on the party, so her source **was** the landlord (if P then Q, not Q, so not P).

Clue 3: the gym news came from the paper. Priya's source is the landlord, Dana's isn't the paper (clue 4) and Leo didn't pass on the gym news (clue 5), so **Sam** passed on the gym news from the **local paper**.

Clue 6: the screenshot rumour is the café. Priya (landlord) can't have the café, and she didn't pass on the party, so she has **rent**. Leo didn't pass on the café, so he has the **party** and Dana has the **café**, from the **screenshot**. Leo is left with the **friend of a friend**.

steps.prompt: Office rule: *If you're working from home, you must join the 9 a.m. call.* Kai joined the 9 a.m. call. What can you conclude for certain?
choices: Nothing about where Kai is working today
Kai is working from home
Kai is in the office
Kai broke the rule
steps.explanation: The rule only says *home → on the call*. Office workers can join the call too, so being on it doesn't tell you where Kai is. Concluding *"so Kai's at home"* is affirming the consequent. If Kai had **missed** the call, you could safely conclude Kai isn't working from home.

units.title: Spot the trick
units.description: The common fallacies, and the correlation-causation mix-up.

lessons.title: Arguing with the wrong thing
lessons.takeaway: Straw men, personal attacks and whataboutism all dodge the real point; bring the conversation back to what was actually claimed.

steps.title: Three classic dodges
steps.body:
Some replies *look* like answers but swerve around the actual point.

- **Straw man**: twist the claim into a weaker version, then knock that down. *"You want less takeaway? So you think we should never have fun."*
- **Ad hominem**: attack the person instead of the argument. *"Why listen to Sam about budgeting? He still owes me $10."*
- **Whataboutism**: deflect a criticism by pointing at someone else's fault. *"I leave dishes out? What about Leo's bike in the hall?"*

steps.prompt:
Priya says: *"I think we should order takeaway less often this month, to save a bit of money."*

Order these summaries of her view from **most faithful** to **most straw-manned**.
items: You want us to order takeaway less often this month to save money.
You want us to stop ordering takeaway this month.
You think takeaway is a waste of money.
You think we should never treat ourselves to anything.
steps.hint: For each one, ask: would Priya agree "yes, that's what I meant"? Then ask how far it stretches her words.
steps.explanation:
Each version drifts further: *less often* → *stop* → *always a waste* → *no treats ever*. Straw men are rarely invented from nothing; they're usually small exaggerations piled up.

The test: would Priya say *"yes, that's what I mean"*? Only the first passes.

steps.prompt: Replies from the Flat 4B group chat. Name the dodge, or mark it as a fair reply.

items.text: "Sam wants a cleaner? So he thinks we're all slobs."
"Priya wants us to recycle more. So she wants us sorting rubbish for hours every night?"
"Don't take Dana's advice about the boiler, she failed her driving test twice."
"Leo wants to split bills by room size? He has the smallest room, so ignore him."
"Sure, I forgot the rent reminder, but what about the time you forgot the internet bill?"
"Why should I turn the heating down when the neighbours have theirs on all day?"
"Splitting by room size seems fair for bedrooms, but we all use the kitchen equally, so let's split that part evenly."
"Leo's boiler tip might be right, but he gets paid to promote that brand, so let's get a second opinion."

steps.hint: Does the reply deal with the actual proposal? If not, does it twist the proposal, attack the person, or point at someone else?
steps.explanation:
**Straw men** inflate the request into something silly. **Ad hominem** replies attack the speaker: driving tests have nothing to do with boilers, and Leo benefiting from his idea doesn't make the idea wrong. **Whataboutism** changes the subject to someone else's fault.

The **fair replies** engage with the actual proposal: one improves it, and one notes an incentive *without* dismissing the claim, then looks for independent evidence. More on that line next.

steps.title: Is pointing out bias always ad hominem?
steps.body:
Not quite. When an argument rests on **someone's own word** (*"trust me, this boiler is the best"*), their incentives and track record are relevant: they tell you how much weight their word deserves.

It becomes **ad hominem** when the attack is used *instead of* answering the argument. Reasons and evidence stand or fall on their own, whoever offers them.

steps.prompt: A salesperson says: *"This $60 phone case is the only one that really protects your phone, trust me."* Which reply is fair rather than ad hominem?
choices: "You'd earn commission on it, so I'd like to see an independent drop test before I take your word for it."
"You're on commission, so whatever you say must be false."
"You look too young to know much about phones."
"Salespeople always lie, so the cheapest case is probably the best."
steps.explanation: The commission is relevant because the claim rests on *trust me*, so the fair move is to ask for evidence that doesn't depend on the salesperson. Declaring the claim false because of who said it is ad hominem, and so is mocking their age. "Salespeople always lie" is a sweeping generalisation that still doesn't test the case.

steps.prompt: In a work meeting: *"Our team missed the launch deadline."* A colleague replies: *"Well, marketing missed theirs twice last quarter."* What's the best way to respond?
choices: "That might be worth looking at too, but it doesn't change that we missed ours. What went wrong on our side?"
"Fair point: if other teams miss deadlines too, ours isn't really a problem."
"Let's settle first which team has the worse record."
"You're just being defensive, so let's drop it."
steps.explanation: Whataboutism works by changing the subject. The fix is to acknowledge the other issue briefly, then **steer back** to the claim on the table. Accepting the deflection drops the point, a who's-worse contest swaps one topic for another, and "you're defensive" is an ad hominem of its own.

lessons.title: False choices and slippery slopes
lessons.takeaway: Ask what other options exist, whether each step of a scary chain is really likely, and whether the expert or crowd actually knows this.

steps.title: Four shortcuts
steps.body:
Four shortcuts that skip the thinking:

- **False dilemma**: only two options offered when there are more. *"Premium plan, or no internet."*
- **Slippery slope**: one step will *inevitably* set off a chain of disasters, with no evidence for the links. *"Allow Friday home-working and soon nobody comes in."*
- **Appeal to popularity**: true or good because lots of people believe or do it. *"Millions use this app, so it's safe."*
- **Appeal to authority**: true because someone impressive said so, often outside their field. *"A famous footballer says this diet cures tiredness."*

steps.prompt: Overheard this week. Which shortcut is each one taking?

items.text: "You're either behind this plan or you don't care about the team."
"We renovate the kitchen this year, or we keep living in a dump. Your call."
"Skip one weekly meeting and people will stop talking, deadlines will slide, and the project will collapse."
"Give the kids phones at 12, and next they'll be up all night and failing school."
"Half the office has already put money into this scheme, so it must be legit."
"That restaurant has a queue round the block, so the food must be healthy."
"A famous actor swears by this supplement, so it works."
"My dentist says this electric car is the most reliable one on the market."

steps.hint: Two options only? A chain of disasters? "Lots of people"? Or one impressive person?
steps.explanation: **False dilemmas** hide the middle options (support *parts* of the plan; a cheaper repair). **Slippery slopes** chain disasters together without showing each link is likely. **Popularity**: a queue tells you the food is *liked*, not that it's healthy, and lots of people investing says nothing about whether the scheme is sound. **Authority**: an actor or a dentist has no special knowledge of supplements or cars.

steps.title: When appeals are fair
steps.body:
Not every appeal is a fallacy. A **relevant expert** speaking in their own field is good evidence, especially when experts broadly agree: trusting a pharmacist about drug interactions is sensible.

It becomes a fallacy when the authority is **outside their field**, stands to gain, or is treated as proof that ends the discussion. Same with crowds: popularity can tell you something is *liked*, not that it's *true* or *safe*. And a slope is only slippery if nobody shows each step is likely.

steps.prompt: Dana wants to try a sleep supplement. Rank these from the **weakest** to the **strongest** reason to believe it works.
items: An actor in a paid advert says it changed her life
A doctor on a talk show says some of her patients liked it
One small study of 30 people found they slept a little longer
A review pooling many large trials found a small but consistent effect
steps.hint: Ask two things of each: does the source know about sleep, and did anyone compare people who took it with people who didn't?
steps.explanation:
The **actor** has no relevant expertise and is paid. The **doctor** knows medicine, but "some patients liked it" is anecdote, with no comparison to people who didn't take it. The **small study** actually measured and compared, but 30 people is few, so chance could explain it. The **review of many trials** is strongest: many independent tests pointing the same way.

Notice that even the best evidence found only a *small* effect. Strong evidence and a big effect aren't the same thing.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: *"Either we all work this weekend or we lose the client."* What's the most useful first question?
choices: "Are those really the only two options? Could we ask for a short extension or deliver part of it first?"
"Which of the two options do you prefer?"
"Can we vote on the two options?"
"How much is the client worth to us?"
steps.explanation: A false dilemma works by hiding the other options, so the best first move is to put them back on the table. Choosing or voting between the two accepts the framing. The client's value matters, but it doesn't question whether there are only two choices.

steps.prompt: Which of these is **not** a slippery-slope fallacy?
choices: "If we skip the car service again, the brake pads could fail: the mechanic measured them at 2 mm last time."
"If we allow one pet in the flat, next it'll be a zoo and the landlord will evict us all."
"If you eat one dessert, you'll never stick to a healthy habit again."
"If the team gets free snacks, soon they'll expect free everything and the company will go bust."
steps.hint: A slippery slope is a chain of unsupported steps. Look for the one with a single step and actual evidence.
steps.explanation: The car warning is one short step backed by evidence (a measurement), so it's a reasonable prediction, not a slope. The other three jump through several unlikely steps to a disaster without showing why each would happen.

lessons.title: Ice cream doesn't cause sunburn
lessons.takeaway: When two things move together, check for a third factor, a reversed arrow or plain chance before believing one causes the other.

steps.title: Moving together isn't causing
steps.body:
Ice cream sales and sunburns rise and fall together. Does ice cream cause sunburn? No: **sunny weather** drives both. A hidden third factor like that is a **confounder**.

When two things are **correlated** (move together), there are four usual suspects:

- A causes B.
- **B causes A** (reverse causation).
- **Something else causes both** (a confounder).
- **Chance**, especially with small or cherry-picked data.

steps.prompt: Each line reports a link. What's the most likely explanation?

items.text: On days when more ice cream is sold, more people drown.
Children with bigger shoes read better.
People who carry lighters get lung disease more often.
People who use walking sticks fall more often.
People who take headache tablets have more headaches.
Busy restaurants have more waiters.
200 tomato plots were randomly given a new or an old fertiliser; the new-fertiliser plots grew 20% more.
An online shop randomly showed half its visitors a new checkout page; that half completed noticeably more purchases.

steps.hint: Is there a third thing that drives both? Could the arrow point the other way? Or did someone randomly assign the change?
steps.explanation:
**Confounders:** hot weather drives both ice cream and swimming; age drives both shoe size and reading; smoking drives both lighters and lung disease.

**Reverse causation:** people who are prone to falls are given sticks; people with headaches take tablets; being busy is why restaurants hire waiters.

**Probably causal:** random assignment means the groups differ only in the thing being tested, so a clear difference is most likely caused by it.

steps.title: The fair test
steps.body:
The gold standard is a **randomised experiment**: randomly split people (or plots, or website visitors) into groups and change only one thing. Random assignment spreads the confounders evenly, so a clear difference between the groups is most likely caused by the change.

When there's no experiment, ask: *what else differs between the groups?* and *could the arrow point the other way?*

steps.prompt: A school finds that students in the chess club get better maths grades. What's the most important thing to check before saying chess *causes* better maths?
choices: Whether students who were already good at maths were more likely to join
How many chess boards the club owns
Whether chess is popular around the world
Whether a newspaper reported the finding
steps.explanation: Students **choose** to join, so the club may simply attract strong maths students (reverse causation, or a confounder like enjoying puzzles). A fairer test would compare students' grades *before and after* joining, or randomly offer chess lessons to some classes.

steps.title: After it, so because of it?
steps.body:
**Post hoc** (from *post hoc ergo propter hoc*, "after this, therefore because of this") assumes that because B came after A, A caused B.

*"I wore my lucky socks and we won."* *"I took the cold remedy and three days later I felt better."* But most colds clear up on their own within a week or two anyway.

Timing is a clue, not proof. Ask: **would B have happened anyway?**

steps.prompt: Leo's office wonders whether a 15-minute afternoon walk makes people more productive. Put the steps of a fair test in order.
items: Decide what counts as "more productive" and how you'll measure it
Randomly pick which people (or days) get the walk
Run both groups over the same weeks, changing only the walk
Compare the groups, and check the gap is bigger than normal week-to-week ups and downs
steps.hint: You can't compare until you've run it, and you can't run it fairly until you've decided who gets the walk.
steps.explanation: Deciding the measure **first** stops you from picking whichever number looks best afterwards (that would be cherry-picking). Random assignment spreads out confounders like workload or keenness. Running the groups side by side avoids seasonal effects. Last, compare, and make sure the gap isn't just the usual noise.

steps.prompt: Dana: *"Since the new manager started in March, sales are up 15%. She's brilliant!"* What's the best follow-up question?
choices: "Do sales usually rise in spring, and did anything else change in March?"
"Is 15% a big increase for us?"
"Which university did she go to?"
"Does the team like working for her?"
steps.explanation: This is post hoc: sales rose *after* she arrived. Seasonal patterns, a new product or a competitor closing could explain it. Checking what usually happens in spring and what else changed tests the causal claim. Her degree and popularity don't.

units.title: Weigh the evidence (and yourself)
units.description: Samples, sources, numbers and the biases of the mind doing the judging.

lessons.title: Small samples, big swings
lessons.takeaway: Before trusting a pattern, ask how many cases it rests on and which cases are missing from the picture.

steps.title: Two visits isn't a verdict
steps.body:
Sam tried the new noodle bar twice, got a cold dish both times, and declared it *"always terrible"*. That's a **hasty generalisation**: a big conclusion from too few cases.

Small samples swing wildly just by chance. Let's see how wildly. In the next step each coin flip is one customer: **heads** means they loved the place, and the true rate is exactly **50%**.

steps.title: Ten customers at a time
steps.body:
Flip **×10** and note the share of heads. Hit **Reset** and do it again, four or five times. A 30% sample followed by a 70% one is perfectly normal.

Then flip **×1000** and watch the rate settle near 50%. Same coin, same true rate: only the sample size changed.

steps.prompt: Leo asks 10 random colleagues about the new coffee machine: 7 prefer it. Suppose the whole company is actually split exactly 50/50. What's the chance that a random 10-person poll still shows **7 or more** in favour? Give a percentage.
steps.hint: It's like flipping 10 coins. The ways to get exactly 7, 8, 9 or 10 heads are 120, 45, 10 and 1. Divide their total by 2¹⁰ = 1,024.
steps.explanation:
There are 120 + 45 + 10 + 1 = **176** ways to get 7 or more "yes" answers out of 2¹⁰ = **1,024** equally likely patterns: 176 / 1,024 ≈ **17.2%**, about 1 in 6.

So "70% prefer it!" from 10 people is weak evidence. With 100 people, a 50/50 company would show 70 or more in favour only about 0.004% of the time. Bigger samples swing far less.

steps.title: The data you don't see
steps.body:
Two more ways a sample misleads:

- **Cherry-picking**: showing only the cases that fit. A gym ad shows three amazing transformations, not the hundreds of members who changed a little.
- **Survivorship bias**: looking only at what *survived* a filter. "Old buildings were built better": maybe, but most of the badly built ones were knocked down long ago, so the ones you see are the sturdy survivors.

Always ask: **what's missing from this picture?**

steps.prompt: What's the main problem with each piece of evidence, if any?

items.text: "I've been to that beach twice and it rained both times. It's always rainy there."
"Three of my friends got the new phone and love it, so it's the best phone out."
A fund's brochure shows its three best years and leaves out the other seven.
A diet ad features five customers who each lost 20 kg.
"Music was better in the 80s. Today's charts are full of junk."
"Every famous founder I've read about dropped out of college, so dropping out helps."
A survey of 2,000 randomly chosen customers found 64% were satisfied.
500 volunteers were randomly given either an early or a late bedtime, then tested on memory.

steps.hint: Too few cases? Someone picked the best ones? Or the failures quietly disappeared before anyone looked?
steps.explanation: **Too small:** two beach trips or three friends can't tell you about every day or every buyer. **Cherry-picked:** someone chose the flattering cases and hid the rest. **Survivorship:** we remember the 80s songs that lasted, not the forgettable ones, and we hear about dropouts who became famous, not the many who didn't. **Solid:** large, random samples, or random assignment.

steps.prompt: A language school's poster: *"Our graduates earn 30% more than the national average!"* What's the most important missing information?
choices: Who enrols in the first place, and how many dropped out before graduating
How many languages the school teaches
Whether the poster was professionally designed
How long the school has been open
steps.explanation: Two filters hide here. People who can afford the course may already earn more (a confounder), and only **graduates** are counted, so anyone who struggled and dropped out is missing (survivorship). A fair comparison is with similar people who didn't take the course.

lessons.title: Who says so, and how do they know?
lessons.takeaway: Before you believe or share a claim, trace it back: who says so, how do they know, and what do they gain?

steps.title: Three questions for any source
steps.body:
Dana forwards: *"BREAKING: the city is banning cars from the centre next month!!"* Before reacting, ask:

1. **Who says so?** A named person or organisation, or "someone online"?
2. **How do they know?** Were they there, did they measure it, or are they repeating someone?
3. **What do they gain?** Money, clicks, a sale, winning an argument?

A claim is only as strong as the weakest link in the chain back to someone who actually knows.

steps.prompt: How does each source know what it's claiming?
buckets: Firsthand: saw, decided or measured it

items.text: The council's own published meeting minutes
A neighbour who watched the crash from her window
A lab report on a sample of your tap water
A news article quoting the council's spokesperson
A friend telling you what her cousin read online
A screenshot of a post with the name cropped off
An article that says "sources say" without naming any
A viral post: "Doctors don't want you to know this!"

steps.hint: Ask: could this source have seen, decided or measured it themselves?
steps.explanation: **Firsthand** sources were there, made the decision or did the measuring. **Secondhand** isn't bad (good journalism is secondhand), but each link is a chance for errors, so check the link back. **Unclear** sources give you nothing to check, which is a reason to hold off rather than share.

steps.title: Incentives aren't proof of lying
steps.body:
Everyone has *some* incentive, and that alone doesn't make a claim false (that would be ad hominem). Incentives tell you **how hard to check**.

- A company's ad about its own product: look for independent tests.
- A headline written to be shared: read past the headline.
- An expert outside their field: the title counts for little.

The strongest signal is **independent confirmation**: several sources that don't rely on each other, saying the same thing.

steps.prompt: Dana's car-ban message. Put these checks in a sensible order before deciding whether to share it.
items: Pause: it's urgent and emotional, so don't share yet
Find where the claim first came from
Check who that source is and how they'd know
Look for independent confirmation, like the council's own website
Decide: share it, share it with a caveat, or drop it
steps.hint: What do you need to know before you can judge a source? And what do urgent messages try to stop you doing?
steps.explanation: Urgent, emotional messages are built to be shared before anyone checks, so the pause comes first. Then trace the claim to its origin, judge that source, and look for independent confirmation. Only then decide. If the council's site says nothing about a ban starting next month, that's a strong sign it's a rumour or an old proposal.

steps.prompt: A website called *Health Truth Daily* says a common sweetener is dangerous. What's the quickest good check?
choices: Open a new tab and see what independent sources say about the site and the claim
Read the site's About page to see how it describes itself
Check that the site looks professional and has no typos
See how many times the article has been shared
steps.explanation: Professional fact-checkers **read sideways**: they leave the site and see what others say about it. An About page is the site describing itself, polish is easy to buy, and share counts measure popularity (appeal to popularity again), not accuracy.

steps.prompt: Which source has the least reason to exaggerate how long a new phone's battery lasts?
choices: An independent consumer magazine that buys the phones it tests
The phone maker's launch event
An influencer who got the phone free and earns money from the link in their video
A shop's website that sells the phone
steps.explanation: The maker, the shop and the influencer all gain if you buy. That doesn't make them wrong, but it means their claims need checking. A magazine that buys its own test phones and earns from readers' trust has the most to lose from exaggerating.

lessons.title: The mind doing the judging
lessons.takeaway: Your mind tends to favour what you already believe, so look for evidence against yourself and argue with the strongest version of the other side.

steps.title: Your brain takes shortcuts too
steps.body:
So far we've checked *other people's* arguments. The hardest claims to check are your own. A few well-studied tendencies:

- **Confirmation bias**: noticing and seeking out evidence that fits what you already believe.
- **Anchoring**: a first number pulls your estimate toward it, even when it's irrelevant.
- **Availability**: judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
- **Motivated reasoning**: demanding more proof for conclusions you *don't* want than for ones you do.

These are normal, not stupid. Everyone does them.

steps.prompt: Which tendency is at work in each case?

items.text: Dana counts the days she feels great as proof her new diet works, and shrugs off the bad days.
Before buying, Sam searches "why this phone brand is the best".
A jacket marked "was $300, now $150" feels like a bargain, though similar jackets cost $100.
Leo guesses a flat's rent higher just after seeing a $3,000 listing for a much bigger place.
After a week of shark-attack stories, Sam feels sharks are a bigger danger than the drive to the beach.
Two of Priya's friends were burgled this year, so she's sure burglaries are rising, though local figures show a fall.
Leo, a big coffee fan, picks apart a study saying coffee is bad but shares one saying it's good without reading it.
Sam's team lost, so he decides the referee was biased, though he praised the same referee last week.

steps.hint: Is it seeking agreement, a number pulling the estimate, vivid examples, or a double standard that depends on what the person wants?
steps.explanation: **Confirmation bias:** counting the hits and ignoring the misses; searching for agreement. **Anchoring:** the "was $300" and the $3,000 listing pull the judgement, even though they're irrelevant. **Availability:** vivid stories and personal cases feel common; the drive is far riskier, and the figures say burglary fell. **Motivated reasoning:** the bar for evidence moves depending on what you want to be true.

steps.title: Turn the questions on yourself
steps.body:
Three habits that tend to help:

- **Ask what would change your mind.** If the honest answer is *nothing*, it isn't a conclusion, it's a commitment.
- **Look for the opposite.** Search for the best case *against* your view, not just for it.
- **Steelman.** The opposite of a straw man: restate the other side in its **strongest** form, so well they'd say *"yes, exactly"*, before you reply.

Changing your mind when the evidence changes isn't losing. It's the whole point.

steps.prompt: Leo wants the flat to get a dog; Priya is against it. Order Leo's summaries of Priya's view from **straw man** to **steelman**.
items: Priya just doesn't like fun.
Priya thinks dogs are annoying.
Priya's worried a dog would be a lot of work and money.
Priya's worried that with four busy schedules nobody will reliably walk it, our deposit could be at risk, and she'd end up doing most of the work.
steps.hint: Which version would Priya herself sign up to? That's the top. Which one she'd find insulting? That's the bottom.
steps.explanation: The straw man turns her view into a character flaw. Each step up takes her reasons more seriously, and the steelman names the specific, strongest concerns (time, deposit, unfair workload). Now Leo can answer *those*, with a walking rota or a chat with the landlord, and he might even change his own mind.

steps.prompt: Sam has believed for years that his shortcut makes his commute faster. Priya times both routes on 10 different days, and the shortcut is slower on 8 of them. What's the most reasonable response?
choices: Update: the shortcut probably isn't faster, though a few more checks wouldn't hurt
Ignore it: Sam knows his commute better than a spreadsheet does
Keep the belief until the shortcut is slower on all 10 days
Dismiss it: Priya just wanted to prove a point
steps.explanation: Good evidence should move you **in proportion** to its strength: 8 out of 10 timed days is decent evidence for a commute. Demanding a perfect 10 out of 10 is motivated reasoning (a bar he'd never set for evidence he liked), and dismissing Priya's motives is ad hominem.

steps.prompt: You're selling your old bike and hoped for about $150. The buyer opens with *"I'll give you $50."* What's the anchoring risk, and the best defence?
choices: Your counter-offer gets pulled toward $50; check what similar bikes sell for first and name your own number based on that
There's no risk: a lowball offer you can see through has no effect
You'll overreact and ask for far more than the bike is worth, so accept $50 to be safe
Anchoring only affects the person who named the number, so the buyer is the one at risk
steps.explanation: In studies, anchors pull estimates even when people know the anchor is arbitrary, so seeing through it isn't enough. Looking up real prices first gives you your own reference point, and naming your number puts a different anchor on the table.

lessons.title: Numbers that mislead
lessons.takeaway: Turn percentages into counts out of a real number of people, and always ask what the starting point was.

steps.title: Fifty percent of what?
steps.body:
Headline: *"Snack X raises your risk of a stomach bug by 50%!"* Scary, until you ask *50% of what?*

If the risk goes from **2 in 1,000** to **3 in 1,000**, that's a 50% **relative** rise but only **1 extra case per 1,000** people: the **absolute** change.

A similar trap: a rate going from 4% to 6% is up **2 percentage points**, but **50%** higher. Always ask: out of how many, before and after?

steps.prompt: Same snack: the risk rises from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. If 10,000 people eat it, how many **extra** stomach bugs would you expect, compared with if none of them had?
steps.hint: Scale both rates up to 10,000 people: 2 in 1,000 is how many in 10,000?
steps.explanation: Per 10,000 people the risk goes from 20 cases to 30 cases, so **10 extra**. Real, but a long way from what "50% higher risk!" makes you picture.

steps.prompt: Sort each statement: does it give a fair picture, or is it likely to mislead?

items.text: "The risk rose from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000."
"Our rate went from 4% to 6%: up 2 percentage points, or 50% higher."
"64% of 2,000 randomly chosen customers were satisfied."
A bar chart that starts at zero and labels each bar with its value
"Risk DOUBLES!" (it went from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000)
"Crime up 100% in our village!" (from one burglary to two)
A bar chart whose axis starts at 98%, making 98.5% vs 99% look like a huge gap
"9 out of 10 dentists recommend it" (in a survey where they could pick several brands)

steps.hint: Can you tell the starting point and the real size of the change? If not, it's probably built to impress.
steps.explanation: The fair versions give the **starting point**, the **sample** or the **real scale**. The misleading ones use a relative change on a tiny base ("doubles", "up 100%"), a stretched chart axis, or a survey design that makes a number sound like a ringing endorsement.

steps.title: The base-rate trap
steps.body:
A shop's security gate catches **9 in 10** shoplifters and wrongly beeps for only about **1 in 20** honest shoppers. It beeps at you. Are you probably a thief?

The missing piece is the **base rate**: how common shoplifting is to begin with. If it's rare, the false alarms from the huge honest crowd can outnumber the real catches.

The trick that makes it easy: imagine **1,000 real people** and count.

steps.prompt: Out of 1,000 shoppers, 10 are shoplifting. The gate beeps for 9 of those 10, and also for 50 of the 990 honest shoppers. The gate beeps at someone. What's the chance they're actually shoplifting? Give a percentage.
steps.hint: Count every beep first, real ones plus false alarms. What share of all those beeps are shoplifters?
steps.explanation:
Total beeps: 9 real + 50 false alarms = **59**. Shoplifters among them: 9 / 59 ≈ **15.3%**. So about 85% of beeps are false alarms, because honest shoppers outnumber shoplifters 99 to 1.

The gate is still useful (a beep raises the chance from 1% to about 15%), but a beep alone isn't proof. The same logic applies to spam filters, fraud alerts and medical screening.

steps.prompt: An investment company launched 20 funds five years ago. It has since quietly closed the 12 that did badly. Its new ad says: *"100% of our funds beat the market!"* What percentage of the funds it **launched** does that "100%" actually describe?
steps.hint: How many funds are still around to be counted, out of how many that were launched?
steps.explanation: Only the 8 survivors are counted: 8 / 20 = **40%**. The 12 closed funds vanished from the record, so the number looks perfect by design. That's survivorship bias built into a statistic, and with 20 funds a few would likely beat the market by luck alone. Ask: *100% of what, and what got left out?*

steps.prompt: Four headlines about four different risks. Order them by how many **extra people per 1,000** would be affected, smallest first.
items: "Risk DOUBLES!" (from 1 in 100,000)
"Risk up 50%!" (from 2 in 1,000)
"Risk up 2 percentage points" (from 10% to 12%)
"Risk up 10%" (from 40%)
steps.hint: Turn each into a before-and-after count out of 1,000 people. A 10% rise of 40% is 4 percentage points.
steps.explanation:
Convert each to extra people per 1,000:

- Doubling 1 in 100,000 → 2 in 100,000: **0.01** extra per 1,000.
- 2 → 3 in 1,000: **1** extra.
- 10% → 12%: **20** extra.
- 40% up by a tenth → 44%: **40** extra.

The scariest-sounding headline is the smallest change. Relative numbers on a tiny base sound huge; a modest-sounding rise on a big base can matter far more.
